articles.title: The horror of the Cornell rape case is how ordinary it is | Moira Donegan
articles.author: Moira Donegan
articles.summary: Many men rape; many men giggle encouragingly, or shrug indifferently, when their friends rape. Many men rape, and few seem to think that it’s a very big deal Maybe more than anything else, sexual violence is repetitive. Men commit it in patterns: mostly against women who are close by and vulnerable, just below them on some social hierarchy: their assistant, their date, their friend, their daughter, their student, their kid’s babysitter. Men rape for opportunity – because they can – and for status – because it makes them feel good. They rape to impress other men, documenting it on phones for one another’s benefit. Men rape and do not always seem to register much of a difference between the sex they’ve had that was rape and the sex that they’ve had that wasn’t. They rape, often, without seeming to think about it, registering their victims’ unwillingness with vague contempt, if at all. Since then, Pike has been in critical condition and is receiving medical attention, according to her lawyers, and has reignited a fierce debate about the role of the death penalty in the criminal justice system. Among those rattled by the incident is Frank Thompson, the former superintendent of the Oregon State Penitentiary. The state has carried out only two executions over the past 60 years, in 1996 and 1997. Thompson planned and oversaw both of them, including construction of the room where the two men died by lethal injection . When I asked Thompson, 83, who stepped down from the job nearly 30 years ago, about Pike’s botched execution, he told me that he was less concerned about why exactly it went sideways and more focused on the bigger questions it surfaces. articles.author: Peter Suderman
articles.summary: Has there ever been a good movie about climate change? The Day After Tomorrow , from the filmmakers behind Independence Day , was hokey disaster schlock; Don't Look Up , from the director of T he Big Short , was a relentlessly cringey metaphor movie; the little-seen How To Blow Up a Pipeline was somewhat better, but its intendedly sympathetic tale of climate radicalism was an own goal that inadvertently indicted its activist-terrorists as neurotic whack jobs. Interstellar and Project Hail Mary are much better films by any measure, but their status as "climate cinema" is at least arguable. And they are, rather notably, about the importance and vitality of risk taking and human ingenuity in the face of civilizational challenges, not pious lectures about consumption, capitalism, and environmental doom. Smug, self-satisfied lectures about human depravity generally don't make for great movies. Turns out that's true even with a top-tier director and the world's biggest movie star. Digger , the new movie from director Alejandro G. Iñárritu and star Tom Cruise, is a spectacular misfire, conceptually bold and occasionally intriguing, but mostly just an exercise in teeth-grinding awfulness.

articles.summary: Brazil’s election this weekend will reshape the diplomatic strategy of Latin America’s biggest economy, analysts said. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is in effect tied with his main challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, though neither appears likely to win outright in Sunday’s first-round vote, necessitating a runoff. The EU, which spent years working with the incumbent to repair ties that were battered under the leadership of Bolsonaro’s father, will be watching closely, fearing Brasília could pivot harder towards Washington. Neither candidate has a strategy for combatting Brazil’s growing dependence on China for trade, a key issue in the presidential race. One thing is for certain, however: Bolsonaro’s brother has threatened any diplomats whom the family believe “sabotaged” their father’s presidency. — Prashant Rao

But this time is a little different, says Michael Johansson, an epidemiologist at Northeastern University. “This is the most locally acquired cases that we've seen in the state,” he says.
